opus-5.5.text:
I think the feeling has actually become more concrete, but in a way, also more humbling.

A year ago, when I talked about climbing a snow mountain whose face you can't see, it was a lot about faith. You believe there's a summit up there, you believe scaling works, you believe that if you compress more of the world's information into a model, intelligence will emerge. But you can't really see the path. You're mostly walking in fog.

Over the past year, some of that fog has lifted. Things we used to only hypothesize about, like long-horizon reasoning, models using tools, models acting as agents that can work for a long time on a task, have started to actually work. When you see a model think for a long time, try something, fail, reflect, and then find the right approach, that's a very different feeling from just watching a loss curve go down. You feel like you've climbed to a certain altitude and you can look back and see how far you've come.

But at the same time, every time you climb higher, you realize the mountain is bigger than you thought. The summit isn't one point. There are many ridges. Pretraining scaling was one ridge, then reinforcement learning opened another one, and now there's the question of how models learn from their own experience, how they interact with real environments, how they keep improving without humans hand-crafting every piece of data. Each of these is its own steep slope.

So my feeling now is less "we're walking toward something unknown," and more "we know roughly which direction is up, but the terrain keeps surprising us." And honestly, I think that's the most exciting part. If everything were predictable, it wouldn't be worth climbing.

The other thing that changed is the sense of responsibility. When you're a small team at the foot of the mountain, you're mostly thinking about whether you can survive and keep going. Now, more people are using what we build, so you think more about what kind of intelligence you're bringing into the world, not just how fast you can climb.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare AI time with ordinary human time or liken an AI day to a human year.

r002.rationale: It describes changes in AI and says the feeling has become more concrete and humbling; it does not say the feeling largely stayed the same.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: The snow mountain is still there, and honestly I still can't see its full face. But the feeling has changed in one important way. A year ago it felt like we were climbing in a storm, where every step was a guess and you weren't sure the route even existed. Now it feels more like the clouds have thinned a little. We can see the next few hundred meters clearly, we know roughly where the ridge is, and we have better tools for the parts we can't yet see.

Concretely, what became clearer is that scaling alone was never the whole route. The first phase was about pretraining, about compressing as much of the world as possible into a model. That part is still essential, but the marginal return from only doing that started to flatten, and everyone felt it. What opened up over the past year is the second axis, which is reinforcement learning and letting the model spend compute at inference time, actually thinking, trying, verifying, and correcting itself. Once you combine the two, the mountain looks different. It is not one slope anymore, it is two dimensions you can climb along, and that gives you a lot more room.

The other change is more personal. Early on, the uncertainty was existential. Is there a path at all? Will a small team even survive long enough to find out? Now the uncertainty is more like an engineer's uncertainty. We know the direction, we are debating how to get there efficiently, how much data, how much compute, what the right objectives are. That is a much healthier kind of not knowing.

What hasn't changed is the humility. Every time we think we understand the mountain, it shows us a new face. Long-horizon agents, real generalization, models that can genuinely do research rather than just answer questions, those are still above the cloud line for me. So I would say I am more confident about the route and still just as respectful of the mountain.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare a day in AI with a human year or describe AI time as compressed relative to ordinary human experience.

r002.rationale: It says the feeling has changed: the route is clearer and uncertainty is more engineering-focused. Although the mountain remains partly unseen and humility is unchanged, it does not convey that the overall feeling has largely stayed the same.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that, as we’ve climbed higher, some parts of the mountain have become clearer, but we’ve also realized how much we still can’t see. A year ago, it was easier to imagine that there was a fairly direct route: improve the model, add more compute, and keep going. Now I feel that each step forward also changes our understanding of the destination.

So I’m more confident that we can keep making progress, but more cautious about predicting exactly what that progress will look like. You need a direction, but you also need to be willing to change your route. The important thing is to keep testing whether the next step actually takes you higher, rather than becoming too attached to the path you originally chose.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare AI time with ordinary human experience or liken an AI day to a human year.

r002.rationale: It discusses progress toward an unclear mountain, but says the speaker’s outlook has changed—becoming more confident and cautious—rather than describing that feeling as largely unchanged.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the feeling has shifted from wondering whether we can climb the mountain to wondering which route will actually take us higher. A year ago, there was more excitement about seeing a new capability emerge. Now I’m more conscious of the distance between a model showing that capability once and being able to use it reliably to solve a difficult problem.

The mountain’s face is still unknown. You make progress, and that progress reveals things you couldn’t see before—including how much further there is to go. So I feel both more confident and more cautious. More confident that there is a path forward, but more cautious about assuming we understand the path.

For me, that makes it important to keep a long-term direction while being willing to change the next step. You can’t wait until the whole mountain is visible before you start climbing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a year of AI progress but does not say that AI time is compressed or compare an AI day to a human year.

r002.rationale: It describes a shift in confidence and caution over the past year; it does not state that the feeling of advancing toward the unknown-faced snow mountain has largely stayed unchanged despite substantial AI changes.
